name: Soy protein
short: Soy is listed among the 8 most significant food allergens. A case report and a review describe reduced levothyroxine absorption; a 2.7-year trial in postmenopausal women had no major adverse events.
text: A review of soy protein allergy notes that soy is on the Food and Agriculture Organization's list of the 8 most significant food allergens and that at least 16 potential soy allergens have been identified, although clinical and animal studies generally show lower allergic reactivity for soy than for other food allergens. A case report described a woman treated for hypothyroidism after thyroid cancer surgery who needed unusually high doses of levothyroxine while taking a soy protein supplement immediately after it, and who reached target thyroid levels on lower doses once the two were taken apart; a review of 14 trials found little evidence that soy affects thyroid function in healthy, iodine-replete people, but said some evidence suggests soy foods, by inhibiting absorption, may increase the thyroid hormone dose needed by people with hypothyroidism, while also stating that hypothyroid adults need not avoid soy foods, and described a theoretical concern, based on laboratory and animal data, for people with compromised thyroid function or marginal iodine intake. In a 2.7-year placebo-controlled trial in 350 postmenopausal women, there were no major adverse events from isoflavone soy protein, and in a 2-year trial in 93 men after prostate surgery, soy protein did not affect body weight, blood pressure, cholesterol or thyroid hormones compared with a casein placebo. The only interaction named in the cited sources is with levothyroxine.
